title: Niacin and Alcohol: Flushing, Liver Risks, and Hangover Myths
excerpt: Is it safe to take niacin and drink? How niacin flush stacks on alcohol flush, why high doses and heavy drinking strain the liver, and the hangover and flush-out myths.
metaDescription: Is it safe to mix niacin and alcohol? How niacin flush stacks on alcohol flush, liver risks at high doses, and why niacin won't flush alcohol out.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a normal multivitamin-level amount of niacin (vitamin B3) and a couple of drinks is not a dangerous mix for most healthy adults. The problems start with higher doses. Niacin taken as a supplement or a cholesterol drug in the hundreds or thousands of milligrams can cause a hot, red, itchy "niacin flush," and alcohol makes that flush stronger. At high doses niacin can also strain the liver, and so can alcohol, so stacking the two is the part that deserves real caution. Niacin also does not cure or prevent hangovers, and it will not "flush" alcohol out of your system faster.

**The quick rules:** If you take prescription niacin (such as Niaspan or a generic extended-release niacin), the official label advises avoiding alcohol and hot drinks around the time of your dose, because they can make flushing worse. If you take high-dose niacin and drink regularly, talk to your doctor about your liver tests. Don't take a big dose of niacin before a night out to "prevent a hangover" or to beat a test. And if you already flush red when you drink, adding niacin will usually make it worse, not better.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before combining niacin and alcohol if** you take prescription niacin or more than about 35 mg a day from supplements, take a statin or other cholesterol drug, have liver disease or raised liver enzymes, have diabetes, gout, or a stomach ulcer, or drink three or more drinks most days. **Get medical help right away if** you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pain under your right ribs, severe vomiting, fainting, chest pain, or trouble breathing. In an emergency, call 911.

## How Niacin and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Niacin is vitamin B3. You get it from food like chicken, tuna, peanuts, mushrooms, and fortified cereals, and your body can also make some from the amino acid tryptophan. It's needed to build two helper molecules, **NAD** and **NADP**, that hundreds of chemical reactions depend on, including the ones your liver uses to break down alcohol.

At food and multivitamin levels, niacin is just a vitamin doing a vitamin's job. At high doses (usually 500 mg to 2,000 mg or more a day), it acts more like a drug. Doctors have used it for decades to lower triglycerides and LDL cholesterol and to raise HDL cholesterol. At those doses, it interacts with alcohol in three main ways.

### 1. Both make your skin flush, and the effects add up

The niacin flush happens because niacin switches on a receptor in the skin (called GPR109A, also known as HCA2). That triggers the release of **prostaglandins**, chemical messengers that widen the small blood vessels near the skin's surface. More blood rushes to the skin, and you get warmth, redness, tingling, and itching, usually on the face, neck, and chest. It typically starts within 15 to 30 minutes of an immediate-release dose and fades within an hour or two.

Alcohol widens those same surface blood vessels through a different route. Alcohol is first turned into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic by-product, and acetaldehyde along with alcohol itself relaxes blood vessel walls. That's why your face can feel warm and pink after a drink. We explain that in more detail in our guide on [why alcohol makes you feel warm](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-feel-warm).

Two different triggers that both open up the same blood vessels tend to stack. That's why the prescribing information for extended-release niacin tells patients to avoid alcohol and hot drinks around the time of their dose: they can make flushing more intense.

### 2. Both put work on the liver

At high doses, niacin can irritate the liver and raise liver enzymes. This is a known, labeled side effect. It's more common with **sustained-release** or "slow-release" niacin bought over the counter, and serious liver injury has been reported in case reports, especially when people switched from immediate-release to sustained-release niacin at the same dose, or took large doses without medical supervision.

Alcohol also stresses the liver, and regular heavy drinking can lead to fatty liver and inflammation. The label for prescription niacin specifically calls for caution in people who drink substantial amounts of alcohol or have a history of liver disease. Neither substance is likely to cause trouble on its own at normal levels, but high-dose niacin on top of regular heavy drinking is a combination your doctor should be monitoring with blood tests.

### 3. Alcohol uses up the same NAD your body makes from niacin

When your liver breaks down alcohol, both steps (alcohol to acetaldehyde, then acetaldehyde to acetate) use up NAD and turn it into its "spent" form, NADH. A heavy night of drinking shifts that balance a long way, which is part of why alcohol interferes with blood sugar control and fat processing in the liver.

This is where a lot of internet advice goes wrong. It sounds logical that topping up niacin would refill NAD and help you process alcohol faster. But your body doesn't run out of NAD building blocks during a night out. The bottleneck is the speed of the liver enzymes themselves, and taking extra niacin doesn't make those enzymes work faster. There is no good evidence that a niacin supplement speeds up alcohol clearance in people.

## Niacin Flush vs. Alcohol Flush: How to Tell Them Apart

Many people searching "niacin and alcohol" have noticed that both turn them red and want to know which is which, or whether one says something about the other. They look similar but come from different places.

| | Niacin flush | Alcohol flush (including "Asian flush") |
|---|---|---|
| **Cause** | Niacin triggers prostaglandin release in the skin | Acetaldehyde builds up, often because of a less active ALDH2 enzyme |
| **Timing** | 15 to 30 minutes after an immediate-release dose; can come later with extended-release | Often within minutes of the first drink |
| **Feels like** | Warmth, tingling, itching, sometimes a prickly or burning feeling | Warmth and redness, sometimes with a fast heartbeat, headache, or nausea |
| **Usually lasts** | Under an hour or two | As long as acetaldehyde stays high, often for much of the drinking session |
| **Gets better with time?** | Yes, most people build tolerance within a few weeks of regular dosing | No. It reflects your genes and doesn't fade with practice |
| **Harmful in itself?** | Uncomfortable but usually harmless | The flush itself is a sign of acetaldehyde buildup, which research has linked to a higher esophageal cancer risk in people with ALDH2 deficiency who drink regularly |

If you get the alcohol flush, our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) explains the genetics and what actually helps.

### Does niacin make alcohol flush worse?

Usually, yes, if both happen at the same time. A niacin flush and an alcohol flush add together, so taking a high dose of niacin and then drinking is a recipe for a much redder, hotter, itchier face. Niacin doesn't change your ALDH2 enzyme, so it won't affect the acetaldehyde side of things. It just adds a second source of redness on top.

### Can niacin "train" you out of alcohol flush?

No. You may read that taking niacin regularly helps you get used to flushing so drinking won't turn you red. Tolerance to the niacin flush is real, but it's specific to the prostaglandin pathway niacin uses. The alcohol flush comes from acetaldehyde, which is a different process driven by your genes. Getting used to niacin doesn't fix that, and there's no good evidence it reduces alcohol flushing. Masking the redness also wouldn't remove the acetaldehyde that's causing it.

## Does Niacin Help a Hangover?

There is no good evidence that niacin prevents or treats hangovers. You'll see it recommended in hangover "stacks" and recovery drinks, usually on the theory that alcohol uses up B vitamins and NAD. That theory is half right: heavy drinking over the long term can lower B vitamin levels, and alcohol does shift the NAD balance. But a single night of drinking doesn't leave a healthy person deficient in niacin, and topping it up the next morning hasn't been shown to make people feel better.

A small amount of niacin in a multivitamin or B-complex is harmless and won't hurt. A large dose, on the other hand, can make a hangover feel worse:

- **It can upset your stomach.** Nausea, stomach pain, and diarrhea are common side effects at higher doses, and that's the last thing you want when you're already queasy.
- **The flush can feel awful.** Waking up flushed, itchy, and overheated when you already have a headache and a fast heartbeat is no improvement.
- **It can drop your blood pressure a little.** Niacin widens blood vessels, and some people feel dizzy or lightheaded, especially when standing up quickly. Dehydration after drinking makes that worse.

If you want the evidence on what does help, see our guide to [vitamins for a hangover](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover) and our broader guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover). We also cover other supplements people pair with drinking, including [magnesium](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol), [L-theanine](/never-hungover/l-theanine-and-alcohol), [ashwagandha](/never-hungover/ashwagandha-and-alcohol), and [NAC](/never-hungover/nac-and-alcohol), plus [glycine](/never-hungover/glycine-and-alcohol) for sleep and [rhodiola](/never-hungover/rhodiola-and-alcohol) for fatigue.

## Can Niacin Flush Alcohol Out of Your System?

No. This is one of the most common myths about niacin, and it has two versions.

**Version one: niacin helps you sober up faster.** Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, roughly one standard drink an hour for many adults, though it varies from person to person. Niacin doesn't speed that up. The "flush" in the name refers to your skin turning red, not to anything leaving your body faster. Feeling hot and red after niacin is not a sign that alcohol is being cleared.

**Version two: niacin helps you pass a test.** People sometimes take large doses of niacin hoping to beat a breath, blood, urine, or EtG alcohol test. There is no good evidence it works for any of them. Medical toxicology literature has documented people who ended up in the emergency room with liver injury, low blood sugar, or dangerous heart rhythm problems after taking large amounts of niacin to try to beat drug tests. It's not worth the risk, and it doesn't do what people hope.

## Prescription Niacin, Statins, and Alcohol

If you were prescribed niacin for cholesterol, the alcohol question matters more, because you're likely taking a dose high enough to act like a drug and you may also be on a statin.

Some things worth knowing:

- **The label says to avoid alcohol around your dose.** The prescribing information for extended-release niacin advises taking it at bedtime after a low-fat snack and avoiding alcohol, hot drinks, and spicy food around the time you take it, to reduce flushing.
- **Your liver tests should be monitored.** Doctors usually check liver enzymes when starting high-dose niacin and periodically after. If you drink regularly, tell your doctor honestly how much. It changes how they read your results.
- **Statins add a liver and muscle consideration.** Niacin plus a statin can slightly raise the risk of muscle problems and liver enzyme changes. Alcohol on top of that is another reason to be careful. See our guide to [statins and alcohol](/never-hungover/statins-and-alcohol) for the details on that side of things.
- **Niacin is used less often than it used to be.** Two large trials, AIM-HIGH (2011) and HPS2-THRIVE (2014), found that adding niacin to statin therapy did not reduce heart attacks and strokes compared with statins alone, and the HPS2-THRIVE group reported more side effects. Because of that, many doctors now prescribe niacin less often. If you're on it, that's a conversation to have with your doctor, not a reason to stop on your own.

Alcohol itself also affects cholesterol and triglycerides. Heavy drinking is a well-known cause of high triglycerides, which is one of the main things niacin is used to treat. Drinking a lot while taking niacin to lower your triglycerides works against the medicine. Our article on [whether alcohol raises cholesterol](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-raise-cholesterol) covers this.

## Other Ways High-Dose Niacin and Alcohol Overlap

Beyond flushing and the liver, a few other niacin side effects line up with alcohol's effects. These mostly matter at prescription-level doses.

- **Blood sugar.** High-dose niacin can raise blood sugar and make diabetes harder to control. Alcohol can push blood sugar either way, and it can cause low blood sugar several hours after drinking, especially without food. If you have diabetes, the combination makes your numbers less predictable.
- **Uric acid and gout.** Niacin can raise uric acid levels, and so can alcohol, especially beer. If you're prone to gout, the two together raise the chance of a flare.
- **Stomach irritation.** Niacin can irritate the stomach and is used with caution in people with active ulcers. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining too.
- **Dizziness and low blood pressure.** Both widen blood vessels. If you also take blood pressure medicines, you may feel lightheaded or faint, especially when standing up.

## Heavy Drinking and Niacin Deficiency

There's one situation where niacin and alcohol really are connected in an important way: long-term heavy drinking can cause **niacin deficiency**. Severe niacin deficiency is called **pellagra**, and it's known for the "three Ds": dermatitis (a rough, darkened, sun-sensitive rash), diarrhea, and dementia or confusion. In wealthy countries, pellagra is rare, and when it does show up, heavy alcohol use is one of the most common reasons. Drinking heavily can mean eating poorly, absorbing less from food, and using up B vitamins faster.

This is not something a social drinker needs to worry about after a weekend out. It develops over months of heavy drinking and poor eating. But if you or someone you know drinks heavily every day and has a new rash on sun-exposed skin, ongoing diarrhea, or confusion, that's a reason to see a doctor soon. Doctors treat it with niacin under supervision, along with other B vitamins, since people who are low in one are often low in several. Our [vitamin B12 and alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamin-b12-and-alcohol) guide covers another common shortfall.

## How Much Niacin Is a Lot?

Here are the general numbers that matter. These are reference figures, not personal dosing advice.

| Amount | What it means |
|---|---|
| 14 to 16 mg a day | The recommended daily amount for adults (14 mg for women, 16 mg for men), according to the US National Institutes of Health Office of Dietary Supplements |
| 35 mg a day | The tolerable upper intake level for adults from supplements and fortified foods, set mainly to avoid flushing |
| 50 to 100 mg | Common in B-complex supplements. Some people flush at this level |
| 500 to 2,000+ mg a day | Typical cholesterol-lowering doses. Should only be taken with a doctor's supervision |

A few practical points:

- **Check which form you have.** "Flush-free" niacin (inositol hexanicotinate) usually doesn't cause flushing, but there's little good evidence it lowers cholesterol either. **Niacinamide** (nicotinamide) is another form of B3 that doesn't cause flushing and doesn't lower cholesterol.
- **Don't swap forms on your own.** Switching from immediate-release to sustained-release niacin at the same dose has been linked to liver injury in case reports.
- **Count all sources.** Energy drinks, B-complex pills, multivitamins, and "hangover" products can all contain niacin, and the amounts add up.

## Practical Tips If You Take Niacin and Drink

If you take niacin and still want to have a drink, these steps lower the odds of trouble:

1. **Separate them.** If you take prescription niacin at bedtime, don't take it right after a night of drinking. Talk to your doctor about what to do with a dose on a night you've been drinking, rather than guessing.
2. **Keep the drinking moderate.** One or two drinks is very different from five or six, especially for your liver.
3. **Eat something.** A small, low-fat snack with your niacin dose reduces flushing, and food slows alcohol absorption too.
4. **Hydrate.** Both widen blood vessels and can leave you lightheaded. Water helps.
5. **Ask about aspirin.** Some doctors suggest a low-dose aspirin before niacin to reduce flushing, because aspirin blocks prostaglandin production. Aspirin plus alcohol has its own stomach-bleeding risk, so only do this if your doctor has suggested it. Our guide to [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) explains why.
6. **Watch for liver warning signs.** Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, ongoing nausea, unusual tiredness, or pain under your right ribs all mean you should call your doctor.

## When to See a Doctor

Most niacin flushes are harmless, even when they're uncomfortable. But some symptoms mean you should get checked.

**Get emergency care (call 911) if you have:**

- Chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, or fainting
- Trouble breathing, swelling of your lips, face, or throat, or hives spreading over your body (signs of an allergic reaction rather than a normal flush)
- Severe vomiting, confusion, or extreme drowsiness after drinking

**See a doctor soon if you notice:**

- Yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes, dark urine, or pale stools
- Pain or tenderness under the right side of your ribs
- Ongoing nausea, loss of appetite, or unusual tiredness while taking high-dose niacin
- Muscle pain or weakness, especially if you also take a statin
- Higher blood sugar readings than usual, or a gout flare
- A rough, darkened rash on sun-exposed skin, ongoing diarrhea, or confusion in someone who drinks heavily every day

## Where DHM Fits

If you landed here because you hoped niacin would make drinking easier on your body, it's worth being clear about what does and doesn't have evidence. Niacin doesn't speed up alcohol clearance, doesn't reduce alcohol flush, and doesn't prevent hangovers.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, is the supplement most often studied for alcohol-related effects. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest it may support the liver enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde. Human evidence is limited, though a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease reported improvements in some liver markers. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright. It doesn't change how niacin and alcohol interact, and you should check with your doctor before adding it if you take prescription niacin or a statin. If you want to try it, [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) are popular options. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers safety with other medicines.

The most reliable advice is still the plain kind: drink less, drink slower, eat, and drink water.

## The Bottom Line

- The niacin in food or a basic multivitamin is not a problem with moderate drinking.
- High-dose niacin and alcohol both widen blood vessels in the skin, so together they cause a stronger, hotter flush. The prescription niacin label advises avoiding alcohol around your dose.
- High-dose niacin and heavy drinking both stress the liver. If you take prescription-strength niacin and drink regularly, your doctor should know and should check your liver tests.
- Niacin does not cure hangovers, speed up sobering up, reduce alcohol flush, or help you pass an alcohol test.
- Long-term heavy drinking can cause niacin deficiency (pellagra), which needs a doctor, not a self-prescribed megadose.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking niacin?**

At the small amounts in food or a basic multivitamin, a moderate amount of alcohol is not a known problem for healthy adults. With high-dose or prescription niacin, it's different: alcohol makes the niacin flush stronger, and both put stress on the liver. The prescribing information for extended-release niacin advises avoiding alcohol around your dose. If you take prescription-strength niacin and drink regularly, talk to your doctor.

**Does niacin make alcohol flush worse?**

Usually, yes, if they happen at the same time. Niacin causes flushing by releasing prostaglandins in the skin, and alcohol widens the same surface blood vessels through acetaldehyde. The two effects add up, so you tend to get redder, hotter, and itchier. Niacin doesn't change the ALDH2 enzyme behind Asian flush, so it won't reduce alcohol flushing.

**Does niacin help with a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that niacin prevents or treats hangovers. A single night of drinking doesn't make a healthy person deficient in niacin, and a large dose can make you feel worse by causing nausea, an itchy flush, and lightheadedness. A small amount in a multivitamin is harmless but won't fix a hangover.

**Can niacin flush alcohol out of your system?**

No. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, and niacin doesn't speed it up. The word flush refers to your skin turning red, not to alcohol leaving your body. There is also no good evidence niacin helps anyone pass a breath, blood, urine, or EtG test, and large doses taken to try have sent people to the emergency room.

**How long after drinking can I take niacin?**

There's no official waiting time for everyone. For a multivitamin dose, it doesn't really matter. For prescription niacin, the label advises avoiding alcohol around the time you take it, so ask your doctor what to do with a dose on a night you've been drinking rather than guessing. Waiting until the alcohol has cleared, eating a small low-fat snack, and drinking water all reduce flushing.

**Is niacin bad for your liver if you drink?**

At normal vitamin levels, no. At high doses, niacin can raise liver enzymes and, rarely, cause serious liver injury, especially with over-the-counter sustained-release forms. Heavy drinking also stresses the liver. The combination is a reason to have your doctor check your liver tests. Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs need prompt medical attention.

**Can heavy drinking cause niacin deficiency?**

Yes. Long-term heavy drinking is one of the most common causes of niacin deficiency in wealthy countries. Severe deficiency, called pellagra, causes a rough rash on sun-exposed skin, diarrhea, and confusion. It develops over months of heavy drinking and poor eating, not after a weekend out, and it should be treated by a doctor.

**Is it safe to take niacin with a statin and alcohol?**

Ask your doctor. Niacin plus a statin can slightly raise the risk of muscle and liver side effects, and alcohol adds to the liver's workload. Large trials (AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE) found adding niacin to a statin didn't reduce heart attacks and strokes, so many doctors now prescribe it less. Don't stop a prescribed medicine on your own.
